present: Look at where each main address in the list ends up: the list shows it.
problem: The list shows the main address that forwards, not where it ends up (a row holds the page, a detail such as "The canonical URL redirects (HTTP 301)" and that address), so the step sends the reader to look for something that isn't there.
replacement: Open the main address the list shows for a page in your browser, and note the address you end up at.

present: Search engines ignore these links, so only visitors are affected.
problem: Search engines don't ignore the link: they ignore the "#" part and follow the link to the page as usual.
replacement: Search engines still follow the link to the page, so only visitors are affected.

present: Language versions labelled with a code that doesn't exist
problem: "A code that doesn't exist" is untrue of codes the rule flags: es-419 exists (Google doesn't support it), and "en-UK" is two codes that both exist.
replacement: Language versions labelled with the wrong code

present: These pages list their versions in other languages, but label one with a language or country code that doesn't exist.
problem: As the title: "doesn't exist" is wider than the rule.
replacement: These pages list their versions in other languages, but label one with the wrong language or country code.

present: Search engines ignore that entry (an "hreflang" link), so searchers in that language may be shown the wrong version.
problem: "Search engines ignore that entry" is untrue of the text's own example: for "en-UK" Google drops the region and reads the entry as plain "en".
replacement: Google ignores that entry (an "hreflang" link), or reads only its language, so searchers may be shown the wrong version.

present: No language version uses a code that doesn't exist
problem: As the title.
replacement: No language version is labelled with the wrong code

present: That's almost certainly a file your page design loads on every page, such as a font, script or logo.
problem: A font can't be what was found: the rule looks at images, scripts, stylesheets, frames, audio and video only.
replacement: That's almost certainly a file your page design loads on every page, such as a script, style file or logo.

present: No link goes through a forwarding address
problem: Only links to the site's own addresses are checked, so a link to another website that forwards passes, and the line is then untrue.
replacement: No link between your pages goes through a forwarding address

present: Google then keeps the old address in its results, which delays the switch when the move is really for good.
problem: Stronger than the fact: Google treats a temporary move as a weak signal, so the old address can stay, not must.
replacement: Google may then keep the old address in its results, which delays the switch when the move is really for good.

present: Google stops visiting that part until the file answers again, while your main site carries on as normal.
problem: "Until the file answers again" is stronger than the fact (after 12 hours Google falls back on its last good copy for up to 30 days); reference 1 says only "when that happens".
replacement: Google stops visiting that part of the site when that happens, while your main site carries on as normal.

present: The browser can't leave the right space, so text jumps down the page as each image arrives.
problem: Stated as certain. The rule reads only the page's code, so where the site's design sets the size (sentence 4) nothing jumps, and that is most modern sites.
replacement: The browser may not leave the right space, so text can jump down the page as each image arrives.

present: Your site has no rules file for search engines
problem: The rule also fires when only another part of the site lacks the file and the main site has one (the detail lists which): the title then says the opposite of what is so.
replacement: A rules file for search engines is missing

present: Remove tracking codes (the part after a "?") from links between your own pages.
problem: The part after a "?" isn't always a tracking code: on many sites it picks the product or the page, and a reader who strips it breaks the link.
replacement: Remove tracking codes, such as "?utm_source=newsletter", from links between your own pages.

present: Note any plugin, tracking code or banner added to the site lately: one of them is the likely cause.
problem: A guess stated as likely: the rule doesn't know the cause, and there may be nothing new on the site at all.
replacement: Note any plugin, tracking code or banner added to the site lately, as one of them may be the cause.

present: Note any plugin, tracking code or banner added to the site lately: one of them is the likely cause.
problem: As canonical-outside-head: a guess stated as likely.
replacement: Note any plugin, tracking code or banner added to the site lately, as one of them may be the cause.

present: A sitemap was found for the site
problem: The check also passes when the site names a sitemap that is missing or broken (sitemap-error then fires), so "A sitemap was found" can sit beside "A sitemap on your site can't be read: it's missing…". The pair the design warns of, the other way round.
replacement: A sitemap was found, or the site names one

present: 125 characters is a rule of thumb, so a description just over it that reads well is fine to leave.
problem: Calls the limit's number "a rule of thumb" a second time: untrue once the limit is changed in Advanced, and one more number to keep in step.
replacement: The limit is a rule of thumb, so a description just over it that reads well is fine to leave.

present: The rules file for search engines answers with an error on another part of your site: the list names which.
problem: Sentence 1 stands alone in the lists and on the report's first page, where there is no list for "the list names which" to point at; and "another part of your site" doesn't say what kind of part.
replacement: The rules file for search engines answers with an error on another part of your site, such as shop.example.com.

present: Search engines get nothing from a sitemap (a file that lists your pages for them) that they can't read.
problem: The bracket splits "a sitemap … that they can't read": read twice.
replacement: A sitemap is a file that lists your pages for search engines, and they get nothing from one they can't read.

present: It's also called a "meta description", and often comes from a default that the site's design fills in.
problem: Two unrelated ideas in one sentence, and "It" changes meaning halfway.
replacement: The shared text (a "meta description") often comes from a default that the site's design fills in.

present: Load one of the pages on a slow connection and watch whether the text jumps as images appear.
problem: A shop owner can't arrange "a slow connection".
replacement: Open one of the pages on a phone and watch whether the text jumps as the images appear.

present: What you miss is a place to tell them where your sitemap is, and to keep them out of pages with no search value.
problem: "Pages with no search value" is a phrase to look up.
replacement: What you miss is a place to tell them where your sitemap is, and to keep them out of pages such as baskets.

present: Browsers block or change such files (they call it "mixed content"), so parts of the page can break or go missing.
problem: "Change such files" isn't something a reader can picture.
replacement: Browsers block some of these files (they call it "mixed content"), so parts of the page can break or go missing.

present: Under that, a page that still feels quick on a phone needs nothing done.
problem: "Under that" has to be traced back to the 2 MB of the sentence before.
replacement: Below 2 MB, a page that still feels quick on a phone needs nothing done.

present: Pages whose links search engines are told to ignore
problem: Reads twice ("links search engines…"), and says "ignore" where its own text and the links check say "not to follow": two words for one thing.
replacement: Pages that tell search engines not to follow their links

present: No page tells search engines to ignore its links
problem: As the title.
replacement: No page tells search engines not to follow its links

present: Links search engines are told not to follow
problem: Without "that", the first three words read as one name ("links search engines").
replacement: Links that search engines are told not to follow

present: Addresses search engines are told not to visit
problem: Without "that", the first three words read as one name ("addresses search engines").
replacement: Addresses that search engines are told not to visit

present: No page in the sitemap lacks a link from another page
problem: A double negative with "lacks": read twice.
replacement: No page in the sitemap is left with no links to it

present: No set of language versions lacks a fallback page
problem: A double negative with "lacks": read twice.
replacement: No list of language versions is missing a fallback page

present: No language version is one search engines can't show
problem: "Is one search engines can't show" reads twice; its neighbour says "leads to a broken page".
replacement: No language version leads to a page search can't show

present: No image was found that doesn't load
problem: "Was found that doesn't" is two clauses for one fact, and past tense among present ones.
replacement: No image fails to load

present: No sitemap was found that can't be read
problem: "Was found that can't be read": two clauses for one fact.
replacement: No sitemap fails to load or has mistakes in it

present: Fix that sitemap, then check the site again.
problem: "That sitemap" points nowhere: the plain sentence doesn't name it (the technical one does). The same results always list it under sitemap-error.
replacement: Fix the sitemap that can't be read (it's listed as a serious problem), then check the site again.

present: Choose "The whole site" when you start a check, then check the site again.
problem: Reads as two steps where there is one: the choice is made as the check is started.
replacement: Check the site again, and choose "The whole site" when you start it.

present: Tick "Links to other websites" when you start a check, then check the site again.
problem: As url-limit: one step written as two.
replacement: Check the site again, with "Links to other websites" ticked.

present: Tick "Images and other files" when you start a check, then check the site again.
problem: As url-limit: one step written as two.
replacement: Check the site again, with "Images and other files" ticked.

present: Ask your developer to correct the site's main address setting if the sitemap keeps using the old one.
problem: One name for one thing: "main address" is Simple's word for a canonical in every other check; here it means the address the site is set to.
replacement: Ask your developer to correct the web address your site is set to, if the sitemap keeps using the old one.

present: Sitemap lists addresses that can't appear in search
problem: A headline with its article dropped, among titles that name a thing; as a thing it also reads right in the passed and skipped lists.
replacement: Sitemap addresses that can't appear in search

present: Sitemap lists addresses outside its own website
problem: As sitemap-non-indexable.
replacement: Sitemap addresses outside its own website

present: No fallback page for other languages
problem: The only one of the eight language titles that doesn't name a thing; "No fallback page…" beside "Not checked" or a tick reads as a finding.
replacement: Language versions with no fallback page

present: A short title can be exactly right, such as a product name, and then there's nothing to do.
problem: Sentence order: the template puts the cost second and "when it is fine" last; here they are swapped.
replacement: Titles like "Login" or "Products" don't tell a searcher what the page is, or whose.

present: But titles like "Login" or "Products" don't tell a searcher what the page is, or whose.
problem: As above: "when it is fine" goes last.
replacement: A short title can be exactly right, such as a product name, and then there's nothing to do.

present: Forwarded addresses
problem: The glossary's word, and the checks' own, is "a forwarding address".
replacement: Forwarding addresses

present: Every page has its own title
problem: REFERENCE. "Every page has its own title" is printed as good news on a site whose pages have no title at all (title-missing fails, this passes). The writer's other duplicates say "No two pages share…".
replacement: No two pages share a title

present: Every link on the site leads to a working page
problem: REFERENCE. The check covers links to the site's own addresses only, so this line sits, untrue, beside a failing "Links to other websites that don't work".
replacement: Every link between your pages leads to a working page

present: Every link has words to read
problem: REFERENCE. The rule tests only links to the site's own addresses (LinkRules leaves links to other sites before the text test), so a site whose social icons have no label passes with a line that is untrue. Its text also never says when a Notice is fine.
replacement: Every link between your pages has words to read

present: Every page and file on the site can be found
problem: REFERENCE, borderline. Beside a failing "Pages or files that don't answer" or "…fail with a server error", "Every page and file on the site can be found" reads as untrue.
replacement: No page or file answers with a "not found" error

problem: NEW FIELD (recommendation 2). The title is a sentence about the site, which reads as a finding beside "Not checked" or under "Looks for".
replacement: A rules file that search engines can't read

problem: NEW FIELD (recommendation 2). The title is a sentence about the site, which reads as a finding beside "Not checked" or under "Looks for".
replacement: A rules file that fails on another part of your site

problem: NEW FIELD (recommendation 2). The title is a sentence about the site, which reads as a finding beside "Not checked" or under "Looks for".
replacement: A missing rules file for search engines

problem: NEW FIELD (recommendation 2). The title is a sentence about the site, which reads as a finding beside "Not checked" or under "Looks for".
replacement: A site that hides most of its pages from search

problem: NEW FIELD (recommendation 2). The title is a sentence about the site, which reads as a finding beside "Not checked" or under "Looks for".
replacement: A sitemap that can't be read

problem: NEW FIELD (recommendation 2). The title is a sentence about the site, which reads as a finding beside "Not checked" or under "Looks for".
replacement: A missing sitemap

problem: NEW FIELD (recommendation 2). The title is a sentence about the site, which reads as a finding beside "Not checked" or under "Looks for".
replacement: A site that answers at more than one address

problem: NEW FIELD (recommendation 2). The title is a sentence about the site, which reads as a finding beside "Not checked" or under "Looks for".
replacement: A site that isn't secure (no HTTPS)

problem: NEW FIELD (recommendation 2). The title is a sentence about the site, which reads as a finding beside "Not checked" or under "Looks for".
replacement: Missing security settings
